newsitem.title: FRANCE: French far-right leader questioned on brawl.
newsitem.headline: French far-right leader questioned on brawl.

text.p: Jean-Marie Le Pen, fiery leader of France's far-right National Front, was questioned by police twice on Thursday in connection with a brawl during the final days of the parliamentary election campaign, a spokesman said.
Front official Alain Vizier said Le Pen had been questioned at home in the morning about the skirmish last Friday in the poor outer Paris suburb of Mantes-La-Jolie.
He was called later in the day to police headquarters in the nearby town of Versailles for further questioning, Le Pen told reporters outside the building.

The burly 68-year-old Le Pen tussled with a female Socialist election candidate who ended up on the ground during a brawl with anti-Front protesters last Friday while campaigning for his daughter Marie Caroline Le Pen.
Socialist candidate Anette Peulvast and a second individual who was not identified were slightly hurt in the incident.

Peulvast has filed a legal complaint against Le Pen, who said he and his daughter both intended to file countersuits against Peulvast and other unnamed individuals for preventing him from exercising his right to campaign.

Marie Caroline Le Pen lost her bid for a seat in the National Assembly in last Sunday's election. The xenophobic National Front wants to ship home millions of immigrants and reserve jobs and state benefits for native-born French people.
According to a local government spokesman, Le Pen "caught the first person at hand who was being pushed by the crowd -- Mrs Peulvast. He seized her by her blouse and threw her to the ground."

Le Pen later branded the spokesman's comment "slanderous" and said he would sue him as well, though he acknowledged having "slightly pushed" individuals who he said tried to prevent him from "walking freely".
At a news conference at National Front headquarters on Wednesday, Le Pen said he had been lured into the confrontation with protesters and had no regrets about his behaviour.
He said the demonstrators had attacked first and thus bore responsibility for the incident, along with Mantes-La-Jolie police and city officials who did not adequately protect him and his entourage.

"Had I remained silent, had I retracted my claws, people would have said that Le Pen was a coward who was unable to resist the 'democratic pressure' put on him. That would have been unlike me," the former paratrooper said.
The investigation is being carried out under the direction of prosecutors in Versailles, near Paris, police said.

The Front won 14.94 percent in the first round of the National Assembly election, its highest score in a legislative poll, and analysts said it played a crucial role in helping the left defeat the previous centre-right majority by splitting the rightist vote.
But the Front won just one seat in the assembly, where it previously had none.
